claims.text: Conventional powder-metallurgy W–Cu composites contain distinct tungsten and copper phases with relatively sharp interfaces.
A uniformly distributed nanometer-scale ZrC interlayer can be formed at W–Cu interfaces by reactive sintering or by pre-coating tungsten particles with a Zr-based precursor.
The proposed ZrC interlayer will be coherent and bond strongly to both tungsten and copper.
The ZrC-modified interphase will reduce phonon and electron scattering at W–Cu interfaces.
A ZrC interlayer provides better lattice matching and bonding continuity at the W–Cu interface.
Better lattice matching and bonding continuity produced by the ZrC interlayer will reduce interfacial thermal boundary resistance.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial thermal resistance will increase the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
ZrC has high melting-point thermal stability and chemical stability.
ZrC is resistant to radiation-induced damage.
The stability and radiation-damage resistance of the ZrC interlayer will preserve the mechanical integrity and irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
Relative to an otherwise comparable untreated W–Cu composite, a ZrC-interlayer composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity.
Relative to the untreated control, the ZrC-interlayer composite will maintain comparable mechanical strength under reactor-relevant conditions.
Relative to the untreated control, the ZrC-interlayer composite will maintain comparable irradiation tolerance under reactor-relevant conditions.
The proposed benefits require a uniformly continuous ZrC interlayer with an optimal nanometer-scale thickness.
Discontinuous or excessively thick ZrC interlayers may degrade overall composite performance.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement depends on ZrC-layer quality and thickness.
